issues.failure_explanation: F is defined only on [0,∞), so F(−t) for t>0 is outside its domain; the specular derivative Fˢ(0) requires the function to be defined in a neighbourhood of 0. issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Extend the domain of F (and G) to (−ε, ε) for small ε > 0 so that F(−t) and G(−t) are defined; rewrite equation (−2) so that the right-hand side is a specular directional derivative of a properly defined function (e.g. ‖v‖ · Gˢ(0) = ∂ˢ_v f(x)).
issues.overall_effect: The example's two displayed equalities (eq: representation of specular directional derivatives - 1 and - 2) are not well-formed as stated, undermining the illustrated 'weak chain rule' for specular derivatives.

issues.title: Composite-function example: F defined on [0,∞) but F(−t) used; equation (−2) garbled
issues.why_classification: The repair requires redefining the domain of the auxiliary functions and correcting a garbled formula so that both displayed equalities are well-defined; this is a contained but non-trivial fix to the construction.

issues.failure_explanation: The 'only if' direction is false: take f ≡ 0 on any open convex Ω. Then ∇ˢ f(x) = 0 for every x, so ∇ˢ f(x)·(x − x*) = 0 for all x, not only for x = x*. The forward direction (x = x* ⇒ equality) is trivial, but the converse does not hold without strict convexity.

failure_location.quote: The equality holds if and only if $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^{\ast}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'if and only if' with 'if' (stating only the forward direction, which is trivially true), or add a strict-convexity hypothesis to restore the equivalence.
issues.overall_effect: The stated equivalence overclaims: the equality condition does not characterise the minimiser for general convex functions.
issues.title: Optimality corollary: 'if and only if' equality claim is false
issues.why_classification: A one-word deletion (or addition of a standard local condition) restores correctness; the substantive inequality ∇ˢ f(x)·(x−x*) ≥ 0 and its proof are unaffected.

issues.failure_explanation: Two independent defects share the root that the proposition as written and proved does not establish its intended content. (i) The hypothesis already assumes 'f is convex', making the conclusion 'f is convex in Ω' tautological. (ii) In the proof, the first subgradient-inequality step replaces ∇ˢ f(z) with ∇ˢ f(w) without justification, and the second step has the inequality direction reversed (the subgradient inequality gives f(z) ≥ f(x) − ∇ˢ f(x)·(x−z), not ≤) and also swaps ∇ˢ f(x) for ∇ˢ f(z). The correct argument uses ∇ˢ f(z) in both one-sided estimates so that the gradient terms cancel; the written proof does not achieve this cancellation.

issues.overall_effect: The proposition neither states nor proves the intended non-trivial result (subgradient inequality ⇒ convexity); as written it is vacuous and the proof is invalid.
issues.title: Subgradient-inequality-implies-convexity: tautological hypothesis and incorrect proof
issues.why_classification: The repair requires both a statement correction and a non-trivial proof rewrite with the correct choice of evaluation point; it is contained but not a one-line fix.

issues.failure_explanation: The algorithm breaks (halts) when the specular gradient norm exceeds the tolerance η. The intended stopping criterion for an optimisation algorithm is to stop when the gradient is sufficiently small (‖∇ˢ f(x)‖ < η), indicating proximity to a stationary point. As written, the algorithm terminates precisely when the gradient is large, which is the opposite of the desired behaviour and would cause immediate or premature termination in typical runs.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the condition '> η' to '< η' in the IF statement of Algorithm 1.
issues.overall_effect: The pseudocode does not implement the SPEG method described in (mtd: specular gradient method); it would stop at iterations where the gradient is large rather than small.
issues.title: SPEG algorithm: stopping condition inverted
issues.why_classification: A single-character correction (reversing the inequality) restores the intended algorithm; the mathematical convergence result (thm: convergence of the specular gradient method) is stated for the idealised method and is unaffected.

issues.failure_explanation: Identical to the SPEG issue: the algorithm breaks when the stochastic specular gradient norm exceeds η, but the intended stopping criterion is ‖∇ˢ f_j(x)‖ < η (gradient sufficiently small).
